planting.note: Set out container divisions in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Cave-in-Rock was selected from an Illinois upland ecotype and has since become one of the most widely planted switchgrass releases for prairie restoration and conservation plantings across the eastern and central United States.

directions: Cave-in-Rock forms a dense, upright clump of coarse blue-green blades that rises well over head height by late summer, topped by open, airy seed panicles that catch light beautifully at the edge of a meadow planting. Released from seed collected near its namesake town along the Illinois side of the Ohio River, this upland ecotype tolerates a wide range of soils from dry uplands to seasonally moist bottomland and needs no irrigation or fertilizer once established. Foliage turns a warm gold-tan in autumn and stands through winter, providing cover and seed for birds. Cut the whole clump back to a few inches in late winter before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Alamo is a lowland ecotype originally collected in south Texas and grows tallest and most vigorously in the warm, long-season conditions of southern gardens.

directions: Alamo is among the tallest switchgrass releases available, capable of forming towering, coarse-textured clumps that can top nine feet in a single season under warm southern conditions before setting airy, reddish-tinged seed panicles in late summer. Bred from a lowland ecotype gathered in south Texas, it thrives in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast gardens and tolerates periodic flooding along ditches and low-lying beds better than upland switchgrass selections. Its sheer scale makes it best suited to large screens, windbreaks, or the back of a big prairie-style border rather than small gardens. Cut back hard in late winter to make room for the next season's rapid regrowth.

planting.note: Set out divisions in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Kanlow is a lowland ecotype originally collected from a wetland in Oklahoma and performs best where soil stays consistently moist through the growing season.

directions: Kanlow produces tall, vigorous stands of broad blue-green foliage and has become one of the most studied switchgrass cultivars in the country because of its heavy biomass yield, a trait that also makes it an imposing architectural presence in a large native garden. Originally gathered from a low, poorly drained site in Oklahoma, it is naturally suited to rain gardens, pond margins, and other spots that stay damp, though it also tolerates ordinary garden soil once established. Loose, open seed heads appear in late summer and age to a soft tan that persists through winter for visual interest and bird forage. Mow or cut the clump to the ground in late winter before spring growth resumes.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Trailblazer was bred at a Nebraska research station for improved leafiness and stand persistence and adapts readily to typical garden conditions across the central Plains.

directions: Trailblazer forms a tidy, upright clump of narrow blue-green blades that stays more compact and leafier than many older switchgrass releases, a trait its breeders selected for to improve stand quality on the northern Plains. In the garden this translates to a neater, less coarse-textured switchgrass that still delivers the airy, fine seed panicles typical of the species in late summer, aging to warm gold in fall. It is exceptionally cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, making it a dependable choice for prairie-style plantings in colder regions. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Aldous Little Bluestem (Kansas Upland Native Grass)

planting.note: Set out divisions in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Aldous was selected in Kansas from native tallgrass prairie stock and is well suited to dry, unimproved sites where richer soil would cause it to flop.

directions: Aldous grows as a fine-textured, upright clump of blue-green blades typical of little bluestem, turning warm copper-orange in autumn and holding that color through much of winter. It was developed from prairie remnants in Kansas for use in rangeland reseeding, and that tough, drought-adapted heritage makes it an easy, low-maintenance choice for dry native gardens, slopes, and roadside plantings today. Fluffy, silvery seed tufts form along the upper stems in late summer and provide winter interest along with forage for birds. Shear the old clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.
sources: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Pastura Little Bluestem (Drought-Hardy Southwestern Native Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; Pastura was selected in New Mexico for use on dry southwestern rangeland and tolerates heat and low rainfall better than many little bluestem selections bred farther north or east.

directions: Pastura is a shorter, tougher little bluestem selection bred from native stands in eastern New Mexico for resilience on arid, wind-exposed rangeland, and that heritage carries over into an unusually drought-tolerant garden plant. Its fine blue-green foliage stays compact through the heat of summer before shifting to rusty orange in fall, with slender seed heads adding subtle texture above the clump. It is an excellent choice for xeriscapes, gravel gardens, and other low-water plantings in the Southwest and southern Plains where lusher grasses struggle. Trim the dormant clump down to a few inches in late winter before spring growth starts.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Osage was selected from native Oklahoma tallgrass prairie stock and is well adapted to the southern and central Plains.

directions: Osage forms a tall, stately clump of blue-green blades that rises above most companion prairie grasses before sending up bronze-gold, plume-like flower heads in early autumn, a signature feature of indiangrass at its best. Selected from remnant tallgrass prairie in Oklahoma, it is well suited to the heat and periodic drought of southern gardens and needs no fertilizer or irrigation once its roots are established. The warm fall color and airy seed plumes make it a strong vertical accent at the back of a native border, and songbirds work the seed heads through winter. Cut the clump to a few inches above ground in late winter before new shoots appear.

planting.note: Set out divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rumsey was selected from an Illinois ecotype for conservation plantings and is one of the most cold-hardy and widely available indiangrass releases for northern gardens.

directions: Rumsey is a reliably cold-hardy indiangrass selection that forms an upright clump of blue-green summer foliage, turning a rich burnt-orange in fall as tall, golden-bronze flower plumes catch the low autumn light. Drawn from Illinois prairie stock, it has long been a standard choice for tallgrass prairie restorations across the Midwest and brings that same easy, low-input toughness to home gardens. It pairs naturally with little bluestem and switchgrass in a mixed native planting, and its winter-persistent seed heads feed birds through the cold months. Cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.
